pr_title: Fix the calculation of the angular velocity
pr_body:
Fix #63004

before this patch:

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6397893/179704430-35b93c09-a0e6-4d6c-b56a-7232d86fd5c0.mp4

after this patch:

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6397893/179704475-b12bf53f-90fd-474f-8e67-07559bc4b8d5.mp4

## Description

The angular speed calculation was wrong when the rotation speed was not enough.

In `Basis::get_axis_angle`, the first condition tested an epsilon of `0.01`.

For example, by rotating on `Y` by `0.005` radians per frame (which is not that slow as you can see in the video) which correspond to an angular velocity of `(0, 0.600408, 0)`, you end up with a difference for `Math::abs(rows[2][0] + rows[0][2]` of `00999993085861` (and sometime `0019999993965` which explain with in this speed, the cube is moving a bit), so when the value is lower than the epsilon, the function don't return an angular velocity.


test project:  [bug-rotation.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/9139075/bug-rotation.zip)
pr_comments: looks ok to me, @aaronfranke what do you think?
I assume this might be needed for `3.x` too? It has the same code.
@akien-mga indeed, the bug is also present in 3.x.
Is what we see in the "after_fix" video expected behavior? The cube doesn't rotate with the platform and is always facing the same world-space direction.
@and-rad Yes, currently only rotation velocity (displacement) is taken into account. I proposed to add the rotation (angle) as well in the near future.
@fabriceci hey, is the rotation bug got fixed? It looks still there in 4.3 stable.

issue_context.title: Player's "CharacterBody3D" doesn't rotate with Platforms
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

v4.0.alpha11.official [afdae67cc] (Alpha Unstable Build)

### System information

Windows10 64bit, Vulkan, RTX 2080 Super

### Issue description

I noticed that the Player's CharacterBody3D is not rotating along with platforms that are also CharacterBody3D. In the (In-Progress) Documentation, it says:

`Moves the body based on velocity. If the body collides with another, it will slide along the other body rather than stop immediately. If the other body is a CharacterBody3D or RigidDynamicBody3D, it will also be affected by the motion of the other body. You can use this to make moving and rotating platforms, or to make nodes push other nodes.`

![RotationBug](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5027750/179056721-2bb80db9-1a4d-4184-81dd-e7a5d0d2f24c.gif)

Through the Gif shown above, it kinda does rotate along with the platform... SLOWLY. I can also share the project file folder in case someone wants to take a look and experiment the bug.


### Steps to reproduce

Create a Node3D, then two CharacterBody3D nodes: One the Player and the other the rotating platorm.

Player's Code should be provided with the built in GDScript Template provided by the engine, while the platform code simply uses `rotate_y(.005)` to rotate.

Control the player and place the player on the rotating platform and you'll be able to see the rotation bug.

### Minimal reproduction project

[Multiplayer_Test.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/9114429/Multiplayer_Test.zip)

review_comments: Note that this is basically `is_equal_approx`, and that method would work better for handling matrices with really big scales (like over a thousand), but I guess that's not such a common case so it's fine to write out a simplified version here which will perform better.

I'm confused as to what this existing code is checking for. If `rows[1][0]` and `rows[0][1]` are within CMP_EPSILON of each other, they are definitely also within 0.1 of each other, so as far as I can tell the first three checks in this `if` statement are always true.

There's addition here, not subtraction. So it seems like it's supposed to check if all of these are close enough to zero (since they are already determined to be close to each other pair-wise). Not sure what's the benefit of checking it like that over checking all of these for being close to zero separately.
Can I consider this resolved? (I can't say more than kleonc)
I'd either rework this or add a comment that basically says what kleonc said... otherwise the next contributor here will get confused again...

> I'd either rework this or add a comment that basically says what kleonc said... otherwise the next contributor here will get confused again...

I wouldn't rework this without actually making sure the reworked code is not worse. It may be done like that for a reason, like maybe it's more numerically-stable or something like that. Not really sure so I would leave it as is for now.
Adding some additional comment is of course fine.

> Not sure what's the benefit of checking it like that over checking all of these for being close to zero separately.

@kleonc Not the n,n row/column ones as this is an identity matrix.

There are already comments explaining the condition (check if it is an identity matrix). What would you like to add? 

I haven't touched this part but the concern I would have is whether `angle_epsilon` is not too big too, it is much larger than a float error.

I don't know why it's tested this way either, I wonder if the test is not weak, for example if there's diagonal 2 0 1, this test might detect it as an identity matrix `(Math::abs(rows[0][0] + rows[1][1] + rows[2][2] - 3) < angle_epsilon`
Since this is just checking for an identity matrix, we can use `is_diagonal` to check that all the other parts are zero.
@aaronfranke Don't you find the test problematic for the diagonal of 1?

> Since this is just checking for an identity matrix, we can use is_diagonal to check that all the other parts are zero.

Yes but the angle_epsilon is way bigger than the one in `is_diagonal`, I don't know if this is ok.
@fabriceci Yes, that code is also very bizzare. It... seems to be just straight up wrong, since it will be true for a basis with a diagonal of `(-5, 7, 1)`.

@aaronfranke Since it sounds weird but we're not sure of anything, I suggest merging this PR which is a low risk one (that will be backported), and then, I can open another one that simplifies the condition.
Sounds good. Also, for your follow-up PR, I just realized, we can use `is_equal_approx(Basis())` to check for an identity.
@aaronfranke Nice one, I just wonder if the first condition (just before the identity one) can be replaced by `is_diagonal` and then we can skip the diagonal test and only check for the 1.

> I don't know why it's tested this way either, I wonder if the test is not weak, for example if there's diagonal 2 0 1, this test might detect it as an identity matrix `(Math::abs(rows[0][0] + rows[1][1] + rows[2][2] - 3) < angle_epsilon`

@fabriceci Not gonna lie, I haven't noticed this last condition before. :laughing: And yeah, it looks absolutely incorrect.

> I just wonder if the first condition (just before the identity one) can be replaced by `is_diagonal` and then we can skip the diagonal test and only check for the 1.

@fabriceci The first condition is meant to check whether the matrix is [singular](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SingularMatrix.html), not whether it's [diagonal](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DiagonalMatrix.html). So no, the first check can't be replaced by `is_diagonal` call.

However, the current check for singularity seems strange/incomplete? :thinking: I mean matrix can be singular / not invertable if this condition isn't met, trivial example:
```
0 0 0
1 2 3
4 5 6
```
So I guess the question is whether there are some assumptions about the actual matrix of the `Basis`. Maybe such matrix is assumed to be invalid / it's assumed to be impossible to obtain such data in `Basis`. But if there are no restrictions then this check would need to be broader. In theory a check for determinant being zero should be sufficient.
